clinicalPearls: The name means 'short trunk'; brachyolmia is a group of dysplasias unified by generalised platyspondyly and short-trunk short stature with relative sparing of the limbs, epiphyses and facies.
It presents in childhood rather than at birth, with a short trunk, scoliosis or kyphosis, sometimes back or limb pain, and normal intelligence.
Traditionally classified into several types: type 1 (Hobaek and Toledo autosomal recessive forms), type 2 (Maroteaux, autosomal recessive) and type 3 (autosomal dominant and more severe).

Autosomal dominant brachyolmia (type 3) is caused by heterozygous TRPV4 variants and sits at the mild end of the TRPV4 skeletal spectrum alongside spondylometaphyseal dysplasia (Kozlowski) and metatropic dysplasia.

An autosomal recessive, brachyolmia-like spondylo(epi)metaphyseal dysplasia is caused by biallelic PAPSS2 variants, which may co-occur with androgen and steroid sulphation abnormalities such as premature pubarche and hyperandrogenism.

Radiographs show platyspondyly with irregular vertebral end-plates and, in the recessive types, 'overfaced' pedicles, while the limbs and metaphyses are largely normal — distinguishing it from spondylometaphyseal and spondyloepiphyseal dysplasias.
The Toledo type has been associated with corneal opacities, so ophthalmology assessment may be relevant.
Because the group is genetically heterogeneous, precise molecular diagnosis guides inheritance counselling and detection of extraskeletal features.
reference.pathophysiology: Brachyolmia is a genetically heterogeneous group unified by generalised platyspondyly with relative sparing of the limbs. The autosomal dominant form (type 3) is caused by heterozygous gain-of-function variants in TRPV4, a chondrocyte calcium-permeable channel, placing it at the mild end of the TRPV4 skeletal spectrum that also includes spondylometaphyseal dysplasia (Kozlowski) and metatropic dysplasia. An autosomal recessive, brachyolmia-like spondylo(epi)metaphyseal dysplasia is caused by biallelic variants in PAPSS2, which encodes the enzyme generating 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulphate (PAPS), the universal sulphate donor; because PAPS is required both for proteoglycan sulphation in cartilage and for steroid (for example DHEA) sulphation, affected individuals may combine short trunk and platyspondyly with signs of androgen excess such as premature pubarche. The historically described recessive types (Hobaek and Toledo, type 1; Maroteaux, type 2) remain partly of undefined molecular basis, and the Toledo type has additionally been linked with corneal opacities.
additionalDifferentials: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, Kozlowski type (allelic with the autosomal dominant TRPV4 form)
Other platyspondylic dysplasias with predominant spinal involvement

redFlags: Neurological signs suggesting spinal cord compression
Features of androgen excess in PAPSS2-related disease
reference.prognosis: Outcome is generally good, with normal intelligence and lifespan; morbidity arises from short stature, spinal deformity and back pain, and from any associated endocrine features in the PAPSS2-related form.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the spinal changes as Scheuermann disease or idiopathic scoliosis
Assuming a single gene or inheritance pattern for what is a heterogeneous group
Missing PAPSS2-related androgen excess and its endocrine consequences
Over-investigating the limbs when the disorder is predominantly spondylar
